label: birds

decision.decided_by: Amit Shenoy, project lead, in his own words to the hub: "Sure do AVes"
decision.relayed_by: hub session scienceclaw-03 to the holdout thread (scienceclaw-93)
reasoning: Aves was chosen knowing it is underpowered for the tests built so far: the held-out bird counts fall below the builders’ own pre-registered minimum sample sizes, so both examined tests read inconclusive.

Mammalia would have made 1 of 2 examined tests decisive, but the examined tests had already fitted on mammal rows, and one further completed test uses mammals only and would have been built entirely on held-out data; a switch now would have made those tests post hoc.
The choice was therefore a clean blind that cannot yet decide over a decisive-looking test on a contaminated design, and the clean blind was taken.

The finding this records is about the data, not the thread: the public trait and demographic tables cannot support a blind clade exam at the builders’ own minimum n for these laws. That is more useful to the next team than a decisive number from a compromised design.

rule: An organism is held out when the inventory's lineage puts it in class Aves (any rank: species, genus, family, order, or the class itself).
The rule is the class, not the list: a bird species that is not in the inventory is held out too.

A taxon above class rank that contains Aves (Animalia, Metazoa, Eumetazoa, Bilateria, Deuterostomia, Chordata, Vertebrata, Craniata, Gnathostomata, Osteichthyes, Sarcopterygii, Tetrapoda, Amniota, Sauropsida, Diapsida, Archosauria, Dinosauria, Theropoda) is excluded from both sides, because its data mixes them.
Everything else is available for building (train).
Genome-ready means the best NCBI assembly is chromosome-level or a complete genome. NCBI's reference flag alone is not enough, because it also marks scaffold-level and contig-level assemblies.
